articles.title: The Letter Company Releases Letterpress-1: A Coding Agent Built for Growth Engineering
articles.content:
The Letter Company has released the beta of Letterpress-1 , a coding agent, harness and IDE for growth engineering. The Letterpress-1 coding agent reads a website and its market, then decides what should exist. It builds the change in a sandbox and opens a pull request with a live preview. TL;DR Size: Letter team says it combines frontier models with fine-tuned small models; names and sizes are not disclosed. Runs on: Letter’s hosted platform against your git repository. No local GPU needed. Setup takes under 5 minutes, per Letter. Performance: No public benchmark. Letter shows 1 self-reported, side-by-side page build against Codex. Best: 760 tools exposed through 1 registry over MCP, REST and CLI. Worst: No measurable eval; entry plan is $100/month with overage at 5x the list rate. What is Letterpress-1? Letterpress-1 is a growth engineering agent from The Letter Company. It turns site and market signals into pull requests. The letter company team argues that websites, unlike apps, react to outside forces. These include agent behavior, Google rankings, human visits and competitor activity . General coding agents were built to scale codebases, not to act on those signals. The agent is aimed at teams that host their marketing site in git. It is proactive: it suggests the next thing to build. Examples include de-anonymization, landing pages, warmed emails, blog automation and agent telemetry. How does Letterpress-1 work? Letterpress-1 runs in 3 modes : Build: create a page or feature from a prompt, with brand copy and visuals kept consistent. Plan: pick a goal and get a build plan of growth actions. Fix: find site issues and dispatch pull requests to fix them. Every change follows the same loop. The agent reads the site, plans and builds in a sandbox. It reviews its own change, then opens a pull request. Each change returns a preview link of your own site . Nothing lands until you choose a preview, a pull request, or a merge after checks pass. Letter team lists 6 surfaces. These are the web platform, a Slack app, the letterpress CLI and a website portal. A standalone app and your own agent round out the list. The in-site IDE works on a live page. Press ⌘L, edit text where you see it, and a pull request follows. Showcase examples also cover A/B tests from live edits. For developers, agents.md documents an MCP server at app.letterstory.com/api/mcp with OAuth. The MCP manifest, OpenAPI spec and API reference form 1 registry of 760 tools. Claude Code, Codex or any MCP-capable agent can call the same functions the app uses. What are Proofs, Simulations, Benches and Phantoms? The launch post highlights 4 primitives aimed at winning over AI agents as buyers: Proofs: signed evidence of customer success, built from telemetry and billing data, for agent visitors. Simulations: mirror versions of your API or MCP with simulated data, so agents can try before buying. Benches: self-hosted, reproducible benchmark apps with open-source code and independent governance. Phantoms: independent, autonomous blogs used to sandbox growth strategies. The site adds more: Kernels, Letterbases, Visitors and Mailers. Then it watches competitor sitemaps and flag new pages. Letter team positions these as replacements for tools like G2, Semrush, Profound, RB2B and Instantly. Play the loop

Where it runs

Plus ⌘L in-site editing: change text on your live page and a pull request follows. 760 tools are exposed over MCP, REST and CLI.

articles.title: Russia wants to camouflage its data centers to stop them being bombed — and it might even move them underground for protection
articles.content: Russian concerns about Ukraine drone strikes have prompted a review of data center resilience to strikes Defense measures include anti-drone nets, signal jamming hardware, and even camouflage The Digital Development Ministry has also proposed moving facilities underground Ukraine’s increasing targeting of Russian data infrastructure has resulted in Moscow considering new defensive measures against drone strikes. The Digital Development Ministry has proposed a list of countermeasures and precautions against attack, ranging from jamming hardware and camouflage to building subterranean data centers. With experts warning that a data center outage could leave a facility value wiped by up to 87%, Russia is taking steps to protect is cloud and AI facilities. But such action could increase costs for each facility by around 10%. Pushing up the potential cost of future data centers, safety measures include protection against shockwaves for servers, power supplies, and cooling systems. Drone strike risk Throughout 2026, Ukraine has stepped up its retaliatory strikes against Russian industrial assets, most recently with five data centers targeted in October. Among these was country’s largest facility, based in ‌Balakovo and owned by Sberbank. Others targeted include three data centers owned by Yandex. At the time, Sberbank First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin told reporters that "We confirm that the data processing center was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption." The Digital Development Ministry recommendations were seen by Russian publication Kommersant , which noted that the ministry had confirmed “The development of recommendations has been completed, the document [...] sent to the relevant organizations.” It appears that the document was initially circulated on October 21 2026, possibly in response to the ‌Balakovo data center strike, and certainly as a reaction to the wider concerns. Kommersant indicates that Russian businesses and citizens are concerned about Ukraine’s targeting of internet infrastructure. Months of downtime Not all data centers are considered to be equal within the plans, which divide the facilities into three categories. K1 indicates strategic targets, K2 is economic targets, while K3 is a signifier of a corporate site. While the exact strategies for each category is unknown, it seems likely that the K1 targets would be subjected to the largest defensive measures. While it might be costly to install shockwave protection, anti-drone nets and signal jammers are likely more affordable elements. The cost of installing shelters and other protections is preferable to the alternative, according to Roman Chustuzian, senior investment director of KAMA FLOW, who told Kommersant: “Even if shelters, grids, sensors and duplication of connections add 5-10% to the cost of the object, it is not comparable with the loss of 87% of its cost and months of downtime.”

articles.title: Apple's Q4 2026 Earnings Call Takeaways
articles.content: Apple held its earnings call for the fourth fiscal quarter of 2026 today, and it was Apple CEO John Ternus' first earnings call in his new role. He had Apple CFO Kevan Parekh on hand, and he brought in Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan. The trio covered iPhone Duo sales, Siri AI, and increasing memory costs, among other topics. iPhone Duo After the earnings release, Ternus told Reuters that Apple isn't able to meet demand for the ‌iPhone Duo‌, and there's no word on when supply/demand balance will be reached. Ternus also acknowledged display issues and said a "very small percentage" of units have been returned. iCloud+ Ternus reiterated Apple's plans to add usage limits on server-side AI features like ‌Siri‌ AI and photo editing. Users who need more capacity will be able to purchase expanded access, but there's still no pricing information or details on the limits included with each iCloud + plan. When asked about token consumption, Parekh said it's still early days on how much is done on-device vs. with Private Cloud Compute. The mix of [on-device and cloud Siri] is very early days, and so it's hard to predict exactly what the mix of those costs are going to look like. Obviously, on device, you know, it's very very efficient. No real costs associated with that. But on the server side, we have some inference costs. I think again, we've just recently launched it and made it available to more users. And so we're in the very very early stages of understanding the kind of mix of those costs, as well as further requirements we might have on the compute side. Siri AI Ternus said Apple has real room to expand ‌Siri‌'s capabilities over time, and that Apple wants customers to be aware of what AI agents have access to. As far as agentic capabilities, you know, we think these are promising tools for users. We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they're giving access to. We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy. So, you know, we're pushing really hard on that with Siri AI, but we're also really encouraged by the fact that Apple devices are the best places to use all forms of AI. He also said Apple's privacy focus differentiates it from other AI providers. I mean, if you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone. You know, whether it's your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that, and Siri can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private, and that nobody else has access to. Even Apple doesn't have access to it, and so we think that is a core kind of differentiator that we're excited about, and we're going to continue to push on that. iOS and macOS Merging With the MacBook Pro gaining a touch display, an analyst asked if we're going to see a single unified operating system in the future. Ternus said Apple tries to make the best version of each and every product, while also adding features like Handoff that span across devices, but the company has no plans to make major changes. If you look at what we did last week with the MacBook Pro, we took a huge leap forward. These MacBook Pros are better in every way than the ones that came before them, and we're really proud of that. And so we don't have any fundamentally different changes that we're planning right now. Nor would we talk about it anyway. China Revenue in Greater China was up 21 percent during the quarter, which was a quarterly record. Performance was primarily driven by the iPhone and the Mac. Install Base Apple has more than 2.5 billion active devices. Memory Ternus said the memory situation is "unprecedented," and Apple expects even higher memory costs in the December quarter. Apple's price increases in June and September offset some of the pressure, as do lower costs from some non-memory components and carry-in inventory. Beyond the December quarter, Apple thinks memory prices will continue to increase . Supply…

articles.title: Apple Dodges Question on More Price Hikes as Memory Costs Climb
articles.content: Apple expects memory costs to continue to increase in the December quarter and beyond, CEO John Ternus said during today's earnings call . Ternus, COO Sabih Khan, and CFO Kevan Parekh all commented on Apple's struggle with memory. "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," said Ternus. He said Apple saw higher memory costs in the September quarter, and the December quarter will be worse. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase," he said. Apple was able to offset September costs by using memory it stockpiled at lower prices and securing lower prices on some non-memory components. Apple expects the same factors to cover some of the December increases, along with price increases on iPads, Macs, and iPhones in June and September. An analyst asked if prices could increase again, but Khan, who took the question, avoided offering a direct answer. Parekh said Apple's price increases were done "reluctantly" and the company is trying to balance the impact. I think what we try to do is evaluate, and in doing that, we evaluate the unit's revenue margin, and we're really being thoughtful and deliberate at evaluating kind of the short-term and long-term considerations. And we really believe we're balancing this well. Ternus said Apple expects a declining benefit from pre-purchasing memory over time. Apple's inventory more than doubled year over year to $14.5 billion, which suggests Apple is buying up memory before prices go up yet again. "As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from June to the September quarter, which you'll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow," he said. Apple expects gross margin to drop from 47.9 percent in the September quarter to 45 to 46 percent in the December quarter, primarily because of higher memory costs, plus some Siri AI costs. Mac and iPad supplies will be constrained in the December quarter because of memory issues. articles.title: Snap Reaches Settlement In Social Media Addiction Lawsuit Ahead of Trial
articles.content: Snap has settled a lawsuit brought by two teenagers who alleged Snapchat was deliberately designed to be addictive and contributed to their mental health problems, avoiding a trial that was scheduled to begin this week. Snap was the last defendant to settle after Meta, Alphabet and TikTok resolved claims in the same case. CBS News reports: The teenage plaintiffs, identified in court documents as S.J. and K.D.B., had alleged in the suit that Snapchat was designed to be addictive and that using the platform from a young age contributed to their mental health issues. "We are glad to reach resolution for our clients," Mark Lanier, founder of The Lanier Law Firm and lead counsel for the plaintiffs, said in a statement to CBS News. "We believe this jury would have found the companies' conduct reprehensible." Snap was the last social media company named in the lawsuit to settle the case, which was set for opening arguments this week. Meta resolved claims last week, while Alphabet and TikTok, the other defendants, each also resolved the allegations. Terms of the Snap settlement were undisclosed [...]. Earlier this year, a jury found Meta and Google-owned YouTube liable in a landmark social media addiction lawsuit, awarding $6 million in damages to a young woman who alleged the platforms' addictive features harmed her mental health. In August, Meta also agreed to pay up to $18 billion in settlements and introduce new child-safety measures to resolve claims from dozens of U.S. states that it deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children while misleading the public about their risks. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: OpenAI built itself a new Git backend, too
articles.content: OpenAI on Monday detailed how it built a new Git backend for its monorepo to power the ever-increasing number of commits its developers and their agents now create. Pando, as the team calls the new backend, cut push latency by nearly 5x, the company says, and it currently serves close to a petabyte of Git data per day at OpenAI. OpenAI is obviously an early adopter of agentic coding tools. Compared to the first quarter of 2024, the quarterly commits to its monorepo will have increased by over 2,400% by the end of this year, the company says. But the issues it is facing are similar to what many other enterprises and Git forges like GitHub are now seeing. With the pace of development increasing, Git itself is becoming a bottleneck. GitHub, for example, spent much of its recent Universe keynote on how it is improving its infrastructure to become faster and more reliable, all while serving billions of pull requests every month. That has given rise to startups like Entire (from former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke) and projects like Origin from Cursor . Like OpenAI’s work, those are based on Git, but others, like Anthropic , basically start from scratch with a new client and architecture. Why OpenAI stayed with Git The OpenAI team explicitly notes that it wanted to retain compatibility with Git. The team was seeing the reliability of its Git backend fall below 90%, with slow fetches and failed merges, but decided to stay within the Git ecosystem. As OpenAI’s Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau, and Ted Nyman ask in the announcement, the question the team asked itself was if it had “reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo?” The answer for OpenAI was that the Git client and protocol weren’t really the problem (though the team is also making some tweaks there), but the way conventional Git servers are built. “For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed,” they write. “When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.” How Pando works Pando drops two things most Git servers treat as requirements. The first is keeping every branch in the repository in a consistent state at once. The second is building a custom packfile, Git’s format for bundling compressed objects, for every client that fetches code. In Git, a branch is simply a pointer to that latest commit. Moving that pointer is the only part of a push that requires coordination. Conventional Git servers order those updates across the entire repository, so when there are many developers working in parallel, a push to one agent’s branch can end up waiting on another’s. Pando, on the other hands, doesn’t coordinate every write across the whole repository. Instead, it handles each branch on its own. Because of this, pushes to unrelated branches then don’t have to wait on each other. There’s a tradeoff here, the team acknowledges. When a client is looking at several branches at once, it may see them at slightly different points in time. In practice, however, users and agents only care about the order of updates to a single branch, OpenAI argues. When a client pushes, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it streams it into blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. It records the new branch tip, the packfile’s location, and its dependencies in a metadata store. By default, Pando advertises only the trunk branch as a base for feature-branch pushes. That makes each pack reusable by other clients that already have the advertised trunk history. Then, when another client fetches the branch, Pando selects the stored packs it needs based on the history it already has. It then returns download links through packfile-uri, a Git protocol feature that lets clients download packs separately. Pando stores the writer’s packfile in blob…

articles.title: Anthropic's compute tab could top $1T as Q3 revenue nears $17B
articles.content: Anthropic has published a regulatory filing revealing nearly $900 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, with additional estimated payments potentially pushing the total beyond $1 trillion. The Monday filing reports that Anthropic expects to pay nearly $70 billion in contractual obligations by September 2027, with a total of roughly $447.5 billion in commitments expected to be incurred by the end of 2030. That's assuming of course its revenues continue their upward trajectory, which the prospectus warns is far from guaranteed. "In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all." "Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the filing reads. Which is to say, if Anthropic's revenues don't grow faster than its compute commitments, it could end up falling into a nasty spiral. And while Anthropic has several options, including debt and equity financing, relying on these long term could dilute existing shareholders or force the company to borrow on unfavorable terms. Every IPO filing reads a bit like this because no company can guarantee eternal success and growth. A lot of this filing's language, as damning as it might sound, is therefore just Anthropic covering its butt. However, even though the company is still growing steadily year-over-year, the latest filing shows revenue growth is already slowing. Between Q1 and Q2 of this year, revenues grew nearly 2.5x. Yet in Q3, Anthropic's reported revenues of nearly $17 billion represented an increase of just 46 percent from Q2. In the same period, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure costs grew 77 percent and it kept signing deals that commit it to more expenditure. Last week, we reported that Anthropic's purchase commitments exceeded $800 billion over the next decade or so. Anthropic now says its commitments are closer to $895 billion. Roughly $320 billion of those commitments relate to existing contractual obligations. Another $451 billion covers leases Anthropic has signed, but that have yet to commence, with the company expecting them to begin between 2026 and 2028, although some remain subject to termination rights or other conditions. Overall, however, Anthropic's compute spend is on track to increase substantially over the next few years. And that's not even counting the blank checks Anthropic has written to secure adequate compute, which it values at $150-$175 billion, putting Anthropic's total compute tab at somewhere north of $1 trillion. Anthropic can't walk away from some of this spending because its deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Broadcom, which now total $437 billion, are non-cancellable. Some require payment regardless of whether Anthropic lights up a single GPU. The AI upstart estimates that of its $895 billion in contracts, only about $213 billion worth allow it to avoid payments. The revised S1 filing also offered insights into the company's customer base, including a major reliance on cloud service providers for distribution. The likes of Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are some of the model dev's biggest compute providers, but according to the filing, cloud marketplaces accounted for roughly 44 percent of its revenue in the nine months ended September 30. Anthropic insists that none of its customers account for more than 10 percent of revenue. Yet reliance on hyperscalers for distribution remains a risk because they are all either actively developing competing products or provide access to models from Anthropic's rivals. Despite all the risks in its prospectus, Anthropic believes it can become a sustainable business if it can access enough compute capacity. And by doing so, the…

articles.title: Apple's earnings were all about unprecedented memory costs
articles.content: A constant issue throughout Apple's latest earnings call was the cost of memory. John Ternus warned several times that the company has only a few ways to minimize the impact for consumers. A Samsung LPDDR5X memory chip - Image Credit: Samsung Even as Apple reported better than expected results in its Q4 earnings call, both Ternus and Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh cautioned analysts about the problems of high memory prices. "Let me give you an overall view on memory," John Ternus said. "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components." articles.title: Mac & iPad will be constrained at least through the end of 2026
articles.content: It's not just iPhone. Apple admits that Mac or iPad supplies are going to be tight for the holiday quarter. Maybe buy now if you see a deal? Orders for some MacBook Pro models are facing delays, thanks to the memory crisis. The fall and holiday sales period is the prime time for Apple, with consumers purchasing its latest releases. However, those in the market for the new iPad mini or a MacBook Pro may face a bit of a delay. During the Apple conference call for its Q4 financial results , Apple confirmed that there will be constraints across the board on Mac and iPad availability, running all the way through the Christmas period. articles.title: The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra releases a patch to fix 'reliability and performance' issues found by reviewers — so should you save your money for now?
articles.content: Microsoft fixes long reboots, screen flicker, and unexpected restarts on the Surface Laptop Ultra Launch reviews revealed slow restart issues even as most of the flicker and crash reports came directly from owners No update can fix the Mini LED panel's slow response, grayish blacks, and weak dimming, or RTX Spark's efficiency limitations Microsoft has shipped the first firmware update for the Surface Laptop Ultra just six days after its RTX Spark-powered flagship went on sale, and the changelog reads like a tidy summary of launch-week grumbles being ironed out. The fix, which was listed in Windows Update as Microsoft Corporation System Hardware Update (200.0.7.0), resolves issues that could cause extended reboot times, screen flickering, and unexpected restarts, and includes a line promising additional bug fixes and performance gains. The rollout is staggered, so not every machine will see it at once, and Microsoft warns that firmware updates can't be uninstalled or reverted once applied, and owners can check for it in the Surface app under Help & support. Six days, three fixes with more unfixable issues to address? Microsoft's speed in addressing the issue seems excellent, but it has more than a few teething issues under the hood. To its credit, this is Microsoft's first Surface with Nvidia's custom silicon and its first with a MiniLED screen, so some teething trouble was always likely, and a patch inside a week suggests the Surface team is watching closely. Zac Bowden of Windows Central , whose review complained about restart times, reports that the reboot problem is now fixed and that the update also targets blue-screen crashes, though he notes those were "something I am yet to encounter on Surface Laptop Ultra anyway." Beyond the unexpected restarts, some reviews noted the flickering issue, while others reported no such issues on their units. These are, however, sadly not the only issues in play: reviewers have also flagged ghosting, battery life, and limits on app and game compatibility on Microsoft's Arm-based platform. The display is where the issues may be most pronounced: Notebookcheck measured a 57 ms black-to-white response time, visible ghosting, and a 0.61-nit black level that leaves dark scenes looking grayish, though its 4,650 Hz PWM backlight frequency should be high enough for most flicker-sensitive users. Its review also reported no local dimming at all, which prompted Microsoft to tell Windows Central that dimming is active by default, with 5,400 Mini LEDs spread across 1,344 zones. Windows Central found that it depends on the "Change brightness based on content" setting and the Enhanced display profile, and that it works best with HDR off. The catch is that HDR off makes ghosting and blooming more visible, while HDR on reduces them at the expense of dimming. Its review summary seems to capture it quite well, stating: "It's just not very good local dimming." Battery life is another key issue: at Computex in June 2026, an Nvidia executive told TechRadar to " expect all-day battery life " from RTX Spark laptops in regular workloads, and Microsoft rates the Surface Laptop Ultra at up to 15 hours of local video playback. Linus Tech Tips measured about nine hours in a 1080p playback test at 200 nits and 60Hz, according to Notebookcheck , the same as a 14-inch MacBook Pro whose battery is 27% smaller, and just 53 minutes under a GravityMark stress load. That is roughly six hours shy of Microsoft's own rating, though the test conditions aren't completely identical, even as Windows Central' s own runs landed at around 14 hours using the Procyon benchmark and closer to 10 in real-world use. Either way, efficiency is a property of the silicon, not something a System Hardware Update rewrites. Some owners have also reported the laptop running warm under light loads, a topic Microsoft has not yet directly addressed. A beta tester for Nvidia silicon or a first mover with an AI advantage? articles.title: Study Claims Vizio Simply Ignores 'Smart' TV Spying Opt Out Requests
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Techdirt: Recently, reports emerged that LG TVs are sniffing around your local network, and even listening to your local environment, even when the TV is purportedly "off." Some of those voice commands were then stored in plain text and uploaded to the internet. LG's response? To deny everything. [...] That latter point is central to a new study out of Northeastern that conducted 5,943 experiments across twelve commercial "smart" TV devices. The researchers found that most smart TVs utilize automatic content recognition (ACR), a technology that captures audio or video snapshots of viewed content and then monetizes that data to help build personalized profiles of viewers. TV makers insist that users are supposed to be able to opt out, but the choice simply doesn't work across a large segment of TVs. Companies like Vizio simply ignored the consumer requests entirely more often than not: "We find that the advertised ACR opt-out fully suppresses ACR-attributable traffic on only four operating systems; on Samsung Tizen traffic consistent with ACR activity persists in more than 60% of evaluated scenarios, and on Vizio SmartCast a content correlated endpoint hosted on Amazon Kinesis continues to receive traffic in 100% of opted-out scenarios." [...] The researchers say since they can't see the precise scope of what's being collected due to encryption, they're unsure whether Vizio is technically violating its FTC agreement (not that we have a current FTC that would care if they were): "The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint; however, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement." Results of whether opting out of ACR tracking actually stopped ACR tracking were all over the map. Roku, for example, ignores opt-out requests when users are watching Roku's own channels. None of the smart TV vendors track Netflix viewing for fear of violating agreements with the streaming giant. Samsung's opt out function was more likely to actually work when a user was watching antenna broadcasts. On two Smart TV platforms, personal viewing data collected by ACR remains unencrypted, despite years of bad press and scandal on the subject. Many appear to be violating the law, but because U.S. regulatory oversight has been gutted, they see no meaningful accountability. That includes smart TV OS' like VIDAA, which is most prominently found on Hisense and Toshiba smart TVs: "VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it. Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can't be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
articles.content: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 . In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices , allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on wa ter systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

articles.title: Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights
articles.content: It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light. Why large dogs age faster In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called "jumping genes," according to a paper published in the journal Science. The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It's part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Music Through Your Cheekbones: How Bone-Conduction Headphones Work and Why They Sound Different
articles.content: Most headphones function in a very simple manner: sound waves created by the headphones propagate through the air into the ear canal and into the inner ear. However, there are some headphones that have a non-traditional approach to producing sound for listening to music. These headphones can deliver sounds through vibrations to the head bones and tissues, thus enabling users to listen to music without inserting earbuds into the ear canals or using bulky headphones that cover them completely. Such headphones are called bone-conduction headphones, as they produce vibrations in addition to the conventional sounds created by speakers. It may appear strange, but the science behind this process is fairly simple. In fact, there is always some kind of bone conduction when a person speaks and hears his own voice. Vibrations generated by the act of speaking pass not only through the air but through the body, which explains why the voice that is recorded differs from the voice we hear when speaking. In addition, transmission of sounds via the head affects how music is being played. In order to explain why this happens, it is necessary to learn more about how these headphones function and how sound vibration turns into music. First, Understand How Traditional Headphones Deliver Sound Before diving into the mechanics of bone conduction, it helps to establish exactly how normal headphones work. Understanding this baseline makes the technical jump to bone conduction much easier to follow. The Journey of Sound Through Your Ears Headphones are designed based on the principle of air conduction and transmit sound into the inner ear in the following way. First, sound waves are produced from the headphones as a result of a diaphragm's rapid vibration. These waves move through the air inside the ear canal and eventually encounter the eardrum that starts vibrating. Then, three small bones in the middle ear, called malleus, incus and stapes, amplify the vibrations and pass them on to the cochlea. It is an incredibly small organ located in the inner ear, which has the shape of a snail and contains fluid. Moreover, it consists of a basilar membrane, which separates the liquid inside the cochlea. As the waves move through the liquid, the sensory hair cells convert mechanical energy to the electrical one. Finally, the signals reach the brain through the auditory nerve, which interprets them as sound. However, the eardrum is not the only place for vibrations to get to the cochlea. How Bone-Conduction Headphones Actually Work Whereas miniature speakers have been traditionally used, modern consumer bone-conduction headphones make use of transducers that are electromechanical. This is because the main function of these transducers is to convert electrical audio signals to mechanical vibration. This is different from normal headphones since the transducer does not go inside or on the ears. They usually come into contact with the skin around the ear region. From Electrical Signals to Mechanical Vibrations Hearing using a bone conduction device is quite distinct from the one used by earbuds. Once the audio signal sent from the computer to the headphones has been received, it gets converted into mechanical waves through the transducer inside. The transducer moves in sync with the skin of your face and the body tissues beneath it. This vibration travels through the biological parts of your head, without interacting with the outer and middle ear at all. Mechanical energy turns into motion in the cochlear region. From here, the entire process becomes just like any other form of hearing process, where the sensory hair cells detect the motion in the fluid and send signals to the brain through the auditory nerve. Does Sound Really Travel Through the Skull Bones? It is easy to picture bone conduction as one simple process involving the skull, but the reality of it is actually quite complicated. articles.title: Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds
articles.content: According to University of Washington research, across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, AI models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest. (BigStock Image) Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead. That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian. Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest. The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance. “Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia , a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study. The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper. The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on. “We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov , a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author. Listen to the five accents below. American: Nigerian: Chinese: Indian: British: The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested. To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline. The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones. The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names , that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views , and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters . The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response. “For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish…

articles.title: Your AI Agent's Memory Needs Two Clocks
articles.content: Consumer agents run for years with the same user. A companion, a coach, or a journaling app collects thousands of small facts, most of which are only true for a while or evolve over time. Things like a race next Sunday, a trial ending in January, a trip last week, etc. With time, the memories stay in the pool even after the event time has passed. Most setups store what the user said and when the system stored it, and nothing about when it actually happened. And the agent has no way to tell what is still true at retrieval time. For continuity, we will use one running example in this article - a fitness coach app called Stride, with a user named Sam. Every memory has two clocks. Event time is when the thing happened: Sam ran the race on Sunday. Write time is when your app got to know about it: during a user’s chat session or during a later data import. Tracking these two independent timelines, when the event happened and when the system learned about it, is bitemporal reasoning , and relational databases have done it for decades. Most memory setups keep only write time, and that holds until the two timelines disagree. They disagree often, and we’ll discuss the list of possible cases here. 1. Loading old history Stride has run for two years and wants to import old chats. Sam wrote "I ran my first 10K last weekend" in June 2025. Store it today, and the system reads "last weekend" against today, so the memory becomes "Sam ran a 10K this week," wrong by a year and stuck that way since the import loses the original date. Pass the original conversation time on every write and resolve the phrase against it. memory.add( [{"role": "user", "content": "I ran my first 10K last weekend, finished in 58 minutes."}], user_id="sam", event_time=1750075200, # 2025-06-16, the day Sam said it ) The stored memory now reads "User ran a 10K on the weekend of 2025-06-14 to 2025-06-15," its created date reads June 2025, and a date filter for June 2025 finds it. 2. Time-relevant terms in chats Sam says "I started the new knee meds yesterday." Resolve the phrase at write time, because only then do you know the actual conversation date, and store the date instead of the word. You also need a precision scale: "yesterday" is a day, "last month" is a month, and you should not invent an exact day from a vague phrase. Pass the exact instant the message was sent so time zones work out. "This morning" sent at 5 AM in Singapore is still the previous day in UTC. 3. Changing facts Sam is vegetarian, then starts eating fish. Sam lives in Lisbon, then moves to Berlin. Both were true at different times, and a coach app that mixes them suggests tofu for lunch recommendations in a city Sam doesn’t live in anymore. Do not delete the old fact. It needs to be retained and linked to the new fact to create a chain of events. A user may ask need the current value or the history depending on different cases: memory.search("Where do I go for dinner this weekend?", user_id="sam") memory.search("Where did I use to go for my weekend runs last year?", user_id="sam") 4. Facts with an end date "Training for the Berlin half on Nov 15" should stop affecting responses after Nov 15. "Dry January" ends Jan 31. Certain memories need an expiration setting at the time of writing, and the expiration should hide a memory rather than delete it, because the record still matters for history. The memory needs to stay visible through the date and drop out of search results the day after, with a way to show expired ones on request. 5. Time-aware retrievals Before each reply, the coach app asks "what did Sam struggle with last week?" or "my knee injury’s progress from July to September." Two tools do different jobs: Filters on actual event times give you hard windows for deterministic questions; that is how a filter on June 2025 would find the memory you created recently in a bulk import. Temporal reranking reorders memories by how well each memory's date fits a natural-language question when an…
articles.author: Rudraj Mehta

articles.titleFa: لزوم وجود دو ساعت در حافظه ایجنت‌های هوش مصنوعی
articles.summaryFa: ایجنت‌های هوش مصنوعی Consumer به مدت طولانی با یک کاربر در ارتباط هستند و اطلاعات متعددی را جمع‌آوری می‌کنند، اما در ذخیره‌سازی، فقط زمان‌های ایجاد اطلاعات را نگه می‌دارند. این مقاله به معرفی مفهوم «استدلال دو زمانی» می‌پردازد که به ایجنت‌ها این امکان را می‌دهد تا زمان واقعی رویداد و زمان ذخیره‌سازی داده‌ها را به طور مستقل دنبال کنند و از اشتباهات در اطلاعات مربوط به زمان جلوگیری نمایند.
articles.summaryEn: Consumer AI agents can interact with a user for years, collecting various pieces of information but often only storing the time the information was captured. This article introduces the concept of 'bitemporal reasoning', which allows agents to track both the actual event time and the time of data capture independently, helping to prevent inaccuracies in time-sensitive information.

articles.title: Your AI Assistant Is Waiting Around - An AI Agent Goes to Work
articles.content: Something clicked for me the day I stopped treating AI like a really smart search box. I have been in AI long enough to have built a company in it and exited it. My old company made ROYBI Robot , an AI robot that taught young children language and STEM, the kind of work that drew real press and put me in rooms I never expected to be in. I say that plainly because it explains my impatience: I have watched AI go through its hype cycles from the inside, and most of my relationship with it still looked like this: I ask, it answers, I move on. A vending machine for words. Useful, sure, but I was still doing all the actual work myself. The chasing down, the compiling, the following up. The AI talked. I acted. Then I learned the difference between an assistant and an agent, and it rearranged how I think about getting things done. An assistant waits for your instructions and executes them. You hand it step-by-step directions. An agent takes a goal and figures out the steps on its own. You give it an objective and some guardrails, and it goes to work while you do something else entirely. The textbook definition says an agent is an AI system that perceives its environment, makes decisions, takes actions, and pursues goals with some degree of autonomy. The practical definition is shorter: an agent is an AI that acts instead of just talking. Here is the analogy that made it click for me. Asking an AI for restaurant recommendations is a chatbot. Hiring someone to research the options, check availability, read the reviews, compare prices, book the table, and put it on your calendar is an agent. Same conversational surface. Completely different animal underneath. The five things that make an agent an agent. Not everything wearing the “agent” label earns it. The word gets slapped on anything with a chat box these days. Here is the checklist I actually use: Perception. It can gather information from its environment: read documents, query a database, watch a feed. Reasoning. It can work through multi-step problems and decide what to do next. Action. It can do things, not just suggest them: call APIs, write files, send messages. Persistence. It keeps context across steps and sessions instead of starting from zero every time. Goal orientation. It is aimed at an outcome, not just answering prompts. Run a few familiar tools through that filter, and the picture sharpens fast. A customer service chatbot that answers questions from a knowledge base? Not really an agent. Give that same bot the ability to check your order in the database, process the refund, update the CRM ticket, and email you a follow-up tomorrow. Now you are talking. And I am not describing this from the sidelines. This is how I run my work today, with my agents working end to end while I direct them and make the calls that actually need a human. Same with coding tools. GitHub Copilot finishing your lines as you type is handy, but it is not agentic. A tool like Cursor, which reads your whole codebase, reasons about the architecture, makes changes across multiple files, runs the tests, and iterates on the failures, is acting, remembering, and pursuing a goal. That is much closer to agency. You do not need all five traits maxed out, by the way. An agent that is strong on three or four of them will still run circles around a plain chatbot. The trick is matching the level of agency to the actual job instead of chasing maximum autonomy for its own sake. The mindset shift nobody warns you about. The hard part of agents is not technical. It is mental. You are used to asking questions and getting answers. With agents, you define goals and turn the AI loose to pursue them. You are used to doing tasks yourself. Now you describe what “done” looks like and let the agent handle the execution. That transition from doing to directing is subtle, and honestly a little uncomfortable at first. You have to learn to specify outcomes instead of procedures, constraints instead of steps. But once it…

articles.title: Apple CEO Ternus Says iPhone Duo Shortages Have No End Date in Sight
articles.content: Apple is unable to meet demand for the iPhone Duo and there's no timeline for when the company will catch up, CEO John Ternus told Reuters following today's earnings report . Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we're not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance. Ternus commented on the display issues some customers have seen, saying that "a very small percentage" of units have been returned and Apple is offering replacements. ‌iPhone Duo‌ orders placed today have delivery estimates in January, and stores have had little stock for online reservations. Last week, Apple said it was aware of an issue impacting the inner display of some units, and it directed customers with an issue to contact AppleCare . Apple reported a September quarter revenue record of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent from last year. Duo sales are not included because the device did not go on sale until after the quarter had ended. articles.title: Apple HomeView Ultra, Drone and Laundry-Folding Robot Reportedly In Development
articles.content: According to The Information, Apple is developing a $1,000 HomeView Ultra smart home hub with a 9-inch touchscreen mounted on a motorized arm that can follow users around a room and autonomously respond to its surroundings. It's also said to be experimenting with more ambitious home robots, including a wheeled robot that follows people, a smart home drone and a machine capable of folding laundry. Notebookcheck reports: According to the report, HomeView Ultra will feature a larger 9-inch touchscreen mounted on a robotic arm. This arm can automatically turn the screen toward the user. With a camera and several sensors, this smart home hub is said to be "fully aware" of its surroundings and capable of acting autonomously. This autonomy ranges from turning on the lights when someone enters the room to shooing a cat away when it jumps onto a table. These sensors are also intended to prevent the arm from hitting nearby objects with the display. Apple is reportedly currently planning to announce this smart home hub in 2027 for around $1,000, but according to The Information, its launch could be delayed until 2028. The reason is allegedly the software, which has not yet been finalized, while the hardware is said to be ready for market already. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: These smart glasses promise to turn your silent mouth movements into text
articles.content: The next time you see a software engineer shaping silent words with their mouth, you may have to think twice before asking if they need a mental health day – they might just be wearing a pair of smart glasses that let them talk to their computer without uttering a sound. Subvocal is a Y Combinator-backed startup aiming to produce these glasses, and already has working prototypes to show off in YouTube videos, including one with YC partner Dave Lieb trying them out and being impressed enough to offer funding. The headset isn’t what the final version will look like, the company notes, which is good: The demo headset is obviously 3D printed and far from fashionable. Once the final product is available it should look a lot sleeker, based on mockups on the company’s website. It’s not clear when they’ll actually be released, though the preorder page says it’ll be sometime in Q1 2027 at an early bird price of $499. It’s not clear what the final full price will be. As for how the glasses work, the founders, Georgia Tech computer science students Aarush Yadav and Arnav Kumar, explain in a launch post on YC that the device uses low-powered radio waves projected from the glasses toward a wearer’s face. Those waves are distorted by muscle movements and the change in a person’s face shape as they speak or simply mouth words, which the duo said can be picked up and translated into written text. “We started working on this about four months ago after building the first version at a hackathon,” the pair explained in their YC post. “Since then, we’ve gone from a table full of electronics and antennas taped to our face to a semi-portable board and sleek glasses that can decode open-ended speech at 200+ WPM and a reasonably low error rate even at a small dataset scale.” This is just a proof of concept, and many key details are still missing, like the accuracy rate, battery life, whether it will paired with an app, or what-have-you. “The core thing we wanted to prove first was that the signal exists and that we can decode it,” Yadav and Kumar said. In a Hacker News post announcing the company, Yadav and Kumar explained that they started the project during the hackathon by focusing on using EMG electrodes attached to Yadav’s face. They didn’t win the hackathon, but apparently the demo was impressive enough to earn some initial funding from San Francisco VC firm Afore Capital. Shortly after that, the pair pivoted from EMG to RF sensing, as a commercial dictation product that required sticking electrodes to one’s face was unlikely to succeed. “Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge,” Yadav said. “First we built an extremely low-noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face.” They eventually got to the functional prototype they have now, and pre-trained the AI models doing the speech recognition to minimize setup time. According to the company, Lieb only had to read 20 sentences to calibrate the headset to his speech patterns. “We think silent speech can become the next interface for interacting with computers, replacing voice and the keyboard,” the company says of its goal. “Emails, prompts, messages, code, notes, commands, all at the speed of speech without bothering anyone around you.” With just four months of work under their belts, Subvocal could be a massive hit, ushering in a new era of silent muttering productivity for workers in a variety of industries, or it could flop as it tries to scale. Those interested in finding out can preorder a pair now for $199, with the other $300 not due until the glasses ship. ®

articles.title: Apple Reports 4Q 2026 Results: $30.7B Profit on $114.5B Revenue
articles.content: Apple today announced financial results for the fourth fiscal quarter of 2026, which corresponds to the third calendar quarter of the year. The quarter included a number of August and September product releases from Apple, as well as the CEO transition from Tim Cook to John Ternus that took place on September 1. For the quarter, Apple posted revenue of $114.5 billion and net quarterly profit of $30.7 billion, or $2.10 per diluted share, compared to revenue of $102.5 billion and net quarterly profit of $27.5 billion, or $1.85 per diluted share, in the year-ago quarter . Gross margin for the most recent quarter was 47.9 percent, compared to 47.2 percent in the year-ago quarter. Apple also declared a quarterly dividend payment of $0.27 per share, payable on November 16 to shareholders of record as of November 12. Apple set September quarter records for total revenue, iPhone revenue, and earnings per share, and an all-time record for Services revenue. For the full fiscal year, Apple recorded $478.8 billion in sales and $132.2 billion in net income, compared to previous record highs of $416.2 billion in sales and $112.0 billion in net income set in fiscal 2025. "Today, Apple is proud to report a September quarter revenue record of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent from a year ago, with iPhone reaching a September quarter record and Services reaching an all-time high, capping off our best fiscal year ever," said John Ternus, Apple's CEO. "We're closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet. That includes the iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original, alongside iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, our most powerful iPhones yet. We also just introduced a whole new generation of hardware for the home and brought Touch to Mac for the first time. Together with the all-new Siri AI, it's an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season." Apple will provide live streaming of its fiscal Q4 2026 financial results conference call at 2:00 pm Pacific, and MacRumors will update this story with coverage of the conference call highlights. articles.title: Third person dies of bird flu since virus started jumping to livestock
articles.content: A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday . It marks the third human bird flu death in the US since a strain of highly pathogenic (H5) avian influenza (HPAI) made the unprecedented jump from wild, migratory birds to dairy cows, which was first reported in the US in March 2024 . The person who died was a Yakima County resident and was said to have had underlying health conditions, which could have made the person more vulnerable to the infection. On Friday, county officials reported that the person was severely ill and hospitalized . In the subsequent announcement of the person's death, officials said they would not be releasing further information about the person, including their name, gender, or age, out of respect for the family's privacy. "Our hearts go out to the individual's family and loved ones during this difficult time," Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. "Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low." Read full article Comments

articles.title: Educational Byte: What Are Synthetic Tokens in Crypto Networks?
articles.content: Something “synthetic” is something artificial by nature, a thing that mimics the “real” version. When we add this term to already artificial tokens, it doesn’t mean that these tokens aren’t “real,” but that they follow the price of another asset. It could be from gold, a national currency, a stock, a commodity, another cryptocurrency, or whatever you want. Still, synthetic tokens aren’t exactly on-chain representations of the referenced asset. If you own a synthetic token that’s tracking the price of gold, this doesn’t give you any ownership of gold itself. It just gives you exposure to the price of the involved asset: If gold rises in price, a synthetic instrument designed to follow it should move in the same direction. That’s a key difference from Real World Assets (RWAs) tokens, which indeed are a loyal representation of a concrete asset in the real world, not only its general price. How Do Synthetic Tokens Work? Smart contracts are at the heart of this type of token. They set the rules for creating, transferring, and managing synthetic positions, while collateral can support those positions. Many systems use overcollateralization, meaning more value is deposited than the value of the synthetic assets created. Overcollaterization is important here because it’s done mainly to manage the risks created by price movements and maintain the synthetic asset's backing. If a synthetic token tracks an asset whose price rises or falls, the collateral needs to provide enough value to support the outstanding synthetic positions . This mechanism creates a buffer between the value of the collateral and the value of the synthetic assets issued, ensuring their existence. Oracles are another important piece of the puzzle. To follow prices, you’ll need precise data, and crypto networks don’t have this precise data natively (unless the underlying asset is native to them). That’s why a smart contract for synthetic assets relies on oracles: they’re data feeds that transform external data into on-chain data. In this case, they bring prices of assets that are completely outside the network, like gold, bonds, or stocks, into the ledger —so the smart contract can read them to calculate values and keep synthetic instruments aligned with their targets. Benefits & Use Cases For a start, a synthetic instrument can provide exposure to an asset or market without requiring the underlying asset itself to move on-chain. That can be useful for commodities, currencies, stocks, and indexes. They can also interact with decentralized applications (Dapps). Because synthetic assets can exist as on-chain instruments, developers can build them into lending systems, exchanges, automated strategies, or other smart-contract applications. This composability gives financial products more ways to interact with one another instead of sitting in separate systems. Derivatives are another natural use case. A perpetual future, for instance, can follow the price of an asset while giving traders a tokenized position that doesn't represent ownership of that asset. Obyte’s Pythagorean Perpetual Futures offer a concrete example. Their tokens follow the prices of currencies, stocks, commodities, or crypto assets using Pythagorean bonding curves and oracle-provided target prices. Because these futures are tokens that track external asset prices rather than represent ownership of those assets, they can be considered synthetic assets . The futures never expire, and their price mechanism adjusts toward the target reported by an oracle. So synthetic tokens cover a broader idea than simply creating a digital copy of something. They turn price exposure into an on-chain, programmable instrument, opening different ways to build financial products around assets that had previously remained outside distributed networks.

articles.title: AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes
articles.content: If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos. Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale. "Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation." Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps. To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as " Legal Zero-Days : A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and " Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System " [PDF]. The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace . Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well." Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code. The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications. Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world. To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm. For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid. Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made. "We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote. "In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves." Wendy Musell, a San Francisco-based employment law attorney and partner, told The Register that the use of AI in the legal field is expanding rapidly. "Some California Courts, including LA Superior Court, are testing the use of AI as law clerks," said Musell. "Generally law clerks would assist the Court by researching and drafting opinions for the judge's review. That means AI is serving that role in certain courts. Litigators now must consider how AI is analyzing motions and cases. "This is the case even where I personally have found different AI sources to appear to have a slant or bias, and often fail to accurately analyze legal issues. It was just a matter of time before AI came for the legislative process." Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register that Ringe's…

articles.title: Developers are downgrading their AI on purpose — and it’s working
articles.content: Anthropic has confirmed that it added new restrictions to Claude Code to prevent users from recreating existing video games. But developers say Claude Opus 5.5 is also refusing reverse-engineering and software-analysis tasks it previously handled, raising questions about what else Anthropic may have changed. For some developers, the refusals are already affecting their work. One developer says paid client projects have stalled because Claude Code won’t work on existing games, while others say the model is refusing to analyze software. At least one developer got back to work by switching to an older Claude model. On Friday, Addy Osmani , a member of Anthropic’s technical team, confirmed on X that the company had deliberately modified Claude Code’s instructions. “We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.” “We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy,” Osmani writes. He clarifies that developers should still be able to create original games, build within established genres and work with their own designs and assets. “We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance,” he adds, inviting developers to contact him if Claude refuses work involving their own creations. Anthropic has not publicly confirmed whether the reverse engineering refusals are tied to the new instructions or to separate cybersecurity restrictions. Reverse engineering hits a wall The complaints extend beyond game development. Developers say Opus 5.5 is refusing software-analysis tasks that previously worked. Technical writer for Phison Electronics USA, Jarred Walton encountered refusals while testing software he was developing, but switching to Opus 4.8 allowed him to continue. While Anthropic is trying to prevent misuse without blocking legitimate development work, developers are left unable to do tasks as Claude Code suddenly refuses what it once handled, with little explanation for the change. developers are left unable to do tasks as Claude Code suddenly refuses what it once handled, with little explanation for the change. Paid client work stalls out On October 30, Ray Weiss , founder and CEO of Conflict Simulations LLC, reported on GitHub that Claude Code had stopped working on paid client projects it had supported for months. His company creates custom digital versions of board wargames for clients who own the physical games. Weiss says the projects use original code and client-supplied materials, but Claude Code now refuses to continue the work because of its restrictions on recreating existing games. Weiss wants Anthropic to distinguish between infringement and commissioned development, offer a verification process, and document major changes to Claude Code’s instructions. The hosted agent risk The complaint highlights a larger problem with hosted coding agents. Anthropic can change what Claude Code will or won’t do without developers changing their code, tools, or prompts. Work that was possible one day may suddenly be blocked the next. Work that was possible one day may suddenly be blocked the next. On October 6, Anthropic expanded its Cyber Verification Program , giving vetted security researchers access to fewer restrictions after acknowledging that its safeguards can block legitimate cybersecurity work. It’s still unclear whether those safeguards are behind the latest refusals, especially since developers say they can complete some of the same tasks using older Claude models. articles.title: SpaceX Is Reportedly Looking At Buying Boost Mobile
articles.content: SpaceX has reportedly held talks with EchoStar about acquiring Boost Mobile or gaining access to its network, potentially giving Starlink a shortcut toward becoming a full-fledged U.S. mobile carrier. Engadget reports: According to Washington Post's sources, the deal could look like SpaceX acquiring Boost Mobile outright or gaining access to its cell network, which is leased from AT&T and T-Mobile. There could be a major hitch with the deal though, since SpaceX's potential mobile service would need the green light from those major mobile carriers, according to the report. The Washington Post also reported that major cell companies, which include AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon, have already turned down Musk down for access to its cell networks in order to launch a separate SpaceX service. Last month, SpaceX reportedly held talks with Crown Castle to access at least 80,000 cellular tower sites across the U.S. as it prepares to launch Starlink Mobile. "We will be building out our terrestrial networks so there's broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call this week. Satellite launches plus spectrum acquisition "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," he said. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
