articles.title: How Timefolk Is Turning Individual Expertise Into Small Group Sessions
articles.content: Some skills are easier to practise when more than one person is involved. A presentation can benefit from an audience. Language practice becomes more dynamic with several voices in the room. Interview preparation can expose people to different questions and responses. Timefolk is extending its skills marketplace around that idea. Through Timefolk , Experts can run small group Events built around a specific skill, with several Clients joining the same practical, in-person session. The format keeps the same basic structure that sits behind the wider marketplace. The skill, city, session fee and number of available places are clear before someone joins. In the app, Clients can find an Event through Explore and see the date, skill, fixed session fee, city and remaining spots on the Event card. They can then join and pay through the app. The purpose is established before the group comes together rather than being decided once everyone arrives. An Expert could run a session around interview practice, Business English, presentation skills, SI tools for work or another practical skill they already use. Several Clients can take part in the same session, creating a different format from an individual session while keeping the activity clearly defined. For Experts, the group model creates another way to share what they know. Instead of running the same type of session individually with several Clients, an Expert can bring a small group together around one skill. The Expert sets the session fee and the number of available places, while Timefolk provides the marketplace and platform infrastructure around the session. For Clients, the value is not only the possibility of a lower session fee per person. The group itself can become part of the experience. Someone practising a presentation can receive reactions from more than one participant, while a language session can include different speaking partners. A career focused session can give Clients the opportunity to hear how others approach the same challenge. The Event still remains tied to one defined skill rather than becoming a general gathering. That distinction is important to Timefolk’s wider positioning as a marketplace for practical, in-person sessions with local Experts. The platform also keeps the same emphasis on structure. Only ID verified members can join an Event, and every Expert and every Client passes a government ID and liveness check before a session. The exact place is provided before the Event, and the venue must be public. Timefolk’s current product material excludes homes, bars and private rooms from the Event format. Timefolk-media-deck The session begins through an Event code or QR, creating a clear point at which attendance is recorded. Timefolk also states that only people who attended can leave a review. Timefolk-media-deck Payments are handled through the app, with Clients able to use methods including Apple Pay, Google Pay or a saved card. Timefolk’s broader payment infrastructure uses Stripe. Timefolk-media-deck The company has also built specific features around the group format. Its current media deck describes a shared Event page, a QR image that Experts can use when promoting the session, a list showing who attended and tools for managing the Event inside the platform. Clients can receive a full refund if an Event is cancelled or if they leave at least 24 hours before it starts. If the time or place changes, the platform provides a window for Clients to leave without charge. Timefolk-media-deck Those details matter because group sessions create different operational questions from individual sessions. The platform needs to show who has joined, how many places remain, what happens if the venue changes and how attendance is confirmed. Timefolk is trying to answer those questions inside the product rather than leaving them to informal coordination. That makes Events more than simply an additional format. They show how a skills marketplace can expand without…

articles.title: I Put My Country's Entire Legal Code in Git: 300,000+ Documents Since 1810
articles.content: This article explains how I built a Git repository of Chile's entire legal code: more than 300,000 laws, decrees and resolutions in a corpus that reaches back to 1810, with one commit per legislative publication, so the text of any law can be read as it stood on any date. It covers scraping the Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN) and LeyChile, building the history with git fast-import, the limits of Git and GitHub that the repository hit, and the web UI, API and MCP server built on top of it. The repository is pisanvs/ley-chile , and you can browse it at leyes.pisanvs.cl . Why Version Control for Legislation? I think most programmers would agree that working—in a team—without a version control system like Git, is as horrifying as ripping your nails out with bare hands. Git has become a ubiquitous tool in the software industry, not because it’s amazing, but because it’s undoubtedly necessary. As coders and hackers, we tend to believe in the delusion that we can fix others’ problems by working our fingers against the keyboard. This is partly (mostly) the reason why one of my obsessions is making other fields of work more efficient. One of these fields of work is law. You see, the lawyers I know religiously use either Google Docs’ or MS Word’s implementations of version control systems. This doesn’t look like a bad idea or use-case at first glance, but upon further examination we can see the shortcomings of this approach. MS Word Git Chronological History ✅ ✅ Author attribution 🚧 (“blame” doesn’t exist, you must rely on version history) ✅ Branching ❌ (need to create a separate file) ✅ Multi-file tracking ❌ ✅ Intentional & Directed commits ❌ “versions” are just point-in-time objects ✅ Can stage specific hunks, write commit messages, explain changes. Selective historical undo ❌ Can only revert to a specific version ✅ Cherry-picking ❌ ✅ Now, we programmers use these features regularly, but other fields of work don’t. They don’t have the tools and they have to find increasingly complex workarounds. A good place to start the Git crusade, in my opinion, is the law. Existing Git Repositories of Laws: US Code and Legalize There are some projects around the world that have tried doing this to varying levels of success. nickvido/us-code nickvido’s us-code repository on GitHub has one substantial shortcoming: it only has 16 commits. How many bills have been passed to modify laws in the US Code? Thousands. At least a few hundred per two-year congressional term. But this doesn’t check out. Why? Because this repo is built from the point-in-time snapshots from the Library of Congress, instead of having its history built per bill. In my humble opinion, although this repo is accurate, it does not provide a value-add over what the Library of Congress snapshots already provide. Legalize.dev Legalize is probably the most complete solution that has scaled this up to multiple countries. But sadly, their Chilean repo is a bit behind: it only has 3k laws and reforms in it, compared to the more than 300k norms in the complete Chilean corpus. I really appreciate the work Legalize has done. If I had been aware of their existence before I started this project, I probably would’ve made a fork instead of starting from scratch. Requirements for a Git-Based Legal Code Repository Apart from being mostly unaware of other solutions, the reason I built this project this way was because I had some very particular requirements and constraints. No good engineering challenge has few constraints, after all! Some of these requirements are considered (rightfully so) a bit outrageous by some friends of mine. I would agree for the most part! It must fully live within Git The code should be as simple and compact as possible Maintainers need not worry about updates to the law The main purpose of these requirements is to have an easily clone-able, replicable and iterable source for the data and the scraper/generator alike. This enables some benefits of distribution and…
articles.author: Maximiliano Morel

articles.title: OpenAI Might Rebrand Its Data Centers As 'AI Compute Campuses'
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else? Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a "PR blitz" for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too. The company's chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be "a bit of a movie trailer for what you're going to see in 2028," when he expects AI to be "the issue" in the presidential election. So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI "speed limits"; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards; and yes -- rebranding data centers as "AI compute campuses." Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments) as "good and healthy." "Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects," he said. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD

articles.title: Powering up for a pivotal moment
articles.content: Utilizing waste carbon at scale, assessing public trust in artificial intelligence and data centers, and building a quantum toolkit for critical applications were among the topics energy experts explored at the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI)’s annual research conference on Sept. 22-23. The complexity of the energy transition demands “a truly interdisciplinary and international approach,” said Paula Hammond, Institute Professor and dean of the MIT School of Engineering, kicking off the conference, which was themed “Transitioning energy at a pivotal moment.” More than 200 people attended Energizing@MIT: MITEI’s Annual Research Conference in person and online, including faculty, scientists, and researchers; representatives of global energy firms; nonprofit organizations; and academic institutions. With the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence and data centers, the challenge of the energy transition grows ever greater, requiring “researchers who can pursue fundamental questions about materials, chemistry, and energy systems … engineers who can design new technologies and determine how they might function at scale … and experts in economics, policy, human behavior, and sociology who can help us understand how those technologies will interact with communities and with the world around us,” said Hammond. From keynote speakers to panelists, seed grant innovators to startup entrepreneurs, the conference featured exemplars in all these categories. Deploying today’s technologies Eric Toone, chief technical officer and managing partner at Breakthrough Energy, set the tone for day one with a keynote address that was clear-eyed in his assessment. “If energy is prosperity,” he told the audience, “at least today, prosperity is emissions.” Yet, Toone was optimistic when he heralded examples of Breakthrough Energy-funded ventures, from iron-air batteries to vacuum-insulated glass windows, which can reduce the carbon costs of energy. “We can absolutely develop new technologies that provide the exact same service, but at zero carbon,” he said. The conference made Toone’s claim tangible as it spanned the full arc of decarbonization — from deploying what we know today to uncovering what may be possible tomorrow. There are “projects that are actually being developed, companies that are putting steel in the ground now, electrons onto the grid to deliver capacity now, or in the very, very near term,” said John Parsons, deputy director for research at the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Parsons moderated a panel on the revival of nuclear fission power. Highlights included Crane Clean Energy Center’s restoration of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear plant, set to restart in mid-2027; work by Électricité de France (EDF) to extend and modernize France’s 57-reactor nuclear fleet, adapting plants to climate impacts; and GE Vernova’s development of mature light-water reactor technology, with a new plant under construction in Ontario. Carbon utilization offers another path to mitigating carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. “The land and ocean are passively taking up almost 50 percent of anthropogenic CO 2 emissions,” said Carolyn Ruppel, MITEI’s deputy director for science and technology, who moderated the panel. “The idea is to find uses for some of the rest of it.” The session showcased research exploring a host of technologies for making products with captured CO 2 . Nicola Ferralis, a research scientist in the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE), highlighted the importance of large-scale uses for carbon waste, such as structural carbon for vehicles and buildings. “We need to find applications that are actually able to match the supply by mass,” he said. Admir Masic, an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and DMSE, described self-heating concrete panels used in real-world conditions in Sapporo, Japan, as well as new concrete materials that can store…

articles.title: Googling "Zelda" today offers a glimpse of how search worked in 1998
articles.content: The year was 1998. Britney Spears topped the charts, Bill Clinton was impeached, and a couple of little websites called Google and Ars Technica came online. It was also the year Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. Google, which has come to dominate the Internet (Ars is still working on that), is celebrating the imminent release of the Ocarina of Time remaster by temporarily transporting us back to that storied year with a search Easter egg. To access the Google time machine, you just have to search for either "Zelda" or "Ocarina of Time." Google will load the standard 2026 results page, but you'll see an animated Master Sword in the lower right corner. It appears on both mobile and desktop—just click the sword and enjoy the show. After a little time-skipping animation and a Link shout (you know the one), you'll swear it's 1998 again. The search page is transformed into a simple list of blue links with retro Google branding. This is particularly apt given the time-shifting mechanics in Ocarina of Time . Read full article Comments

articles.title: Turning Product Info into Video Ads: Our Experience with Vizard Agent
articles.content: Nowadays, having enough product material is rarely the main problem for e-commerce operators. Amazon listings may already contain product images, descriptions, key features, pricing information, and other commercial assets. The harder part is turning those materials into enough video creatives for advertising campaigns without spending hours on scripting, editing, and producing variations. Therefore, we tested Vizard Agent from this perspective, focusing on a common scenario in which an e-commerce operator has plenty of product information but needs to produce a large number of promotional videos. The test looked particularly at its Amazon Product Link to Promo Video workflow, as well as its UGC-style and advertising function. What We Tested The starting point was quiet simple. Instead of preparing a complete video production package, the workflow begins with an Amazon product listing URL. Vizard's Ads mode allows sellers to paste an Amazon listing URL and have Vizard Agent extract product visuals and product details as the basis for video creation. The workflow can also start from uploaded product images, descriptions, and key features when a URL is not the preferred input. This approach fits the broader design of Vizard Agent. The Agent can work with links, existing footage, files, or combinations of user materials and generated assets. It interprets the request, plans the video, selects or creates assets, makes creative decisions, assembles the result, and reviews the finished video. For an e-commerce operator, that changes the starting point considerably. The product listing itself can become the creative brief rather than simply a reference that someone has to manually read before beginning production. From Amazon Listing to Promo Video The workflow is useful because it connects product information with the actual video production process. After providing the listing, the user can specify the desired video type by giving the prompts, such as a product showcase, lifestyle-oriented video, or promotional advertisement. Vizard Agent then adapts the visual treatment to the requested format. Product images and descriptions provide the foundation, while subtitles, voiceover, visual elements, and other creative components can be incorporated into the finished video. This is where the workflow becomes more practical than simply converting an image into a slideshow. The purpose is to turn product information into a structured promotional story. Instead of deciding manually which product feature should appear first, writing the script, selecting supporting visuals, and arranging the scenes one by one, the operator can give the Agent the product and the intended advertising goal. Vizard's documented product-ad workflow also covers product pages to video ads, product images to UGC-style ads, multiple advertising angles for one product, variations from a winning advertisement, and seasonal campaign variations. For high-volume e-commerce campaigns, the ability to move from one product to several creative directions is arguably more important than producing one polished video. UGC Adds Another Layer The UGC mode was one of the more practical parts of the test. We started with the same product materials rather than preparing a separate batch of creator footage, and used the product images as the basis for a UGC-style ad. The result was noticeably different from a conventional product showcase, with the product positioned within a more creator-oriented advertising format. What worked particularly well here was the amount of preparation Vizard Agent handled on its own. We did not have to build a separate UGC script, work out the structure manually, or assemble the product visuals scene by scene. Vizard Agent allows product images to be turned into UGC-style ads and treats the creative process as a broader video-production task rather than a sequence of individual editing operations.From a testing perspective, the more interesting point was…

articles.title: John Ternus Hosting His First Earnings Call as Apple CEO Today
articles.content: John Ternus will participate in his first Apple earnings call as the company's CEO today. The call begins at 2 p.m. Pacific Time / 5 p.m. Eastern Time. Ternus and Apple's CFO Kevan Parekh will discuss the company's earnings results for the third quarter of the 2026 calendar year on the live-streamed conference call. While the call is primarily intended for Apple shareholders and Wall Street analysts, anyone can listen live for free on Apple's Investor Relations website , with no registration required. The call should last around one hour. Ternus and Parekh will read their prepared remarks, and then they will take questions from analysts. Apple released the following products in the quarter, which ran from June 28 to September 26: Mac Mini With M6 and M5 Pro Chips Mac Studio With M5 Max and M5 Ultra Chips New Apple Polishing Cloth iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max Apple Watch Series 12 Apple Watch Ultra 4 AirPods 5 Beats 360 Wrist Strap for iPhone 18 Pro and AirPods Pro 3 New Apple Watch Charging Puck iPhone Duo was announced during the quarter, but pre-orders did not begin until October 16, so the quarter does not include any revenue from that device. If you miss the call, a recording will be available for replay on the page later in the day. articles.author: Joe Rossignol

articles.title: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
articles.content: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Whether you intend to put its many tracking features to the test, or you simply want the longest battery life of any Apple Watch, it’s currently on sale for $699.99 ($100 off) in multiple colors at Amazon , matching its all-time low price. Apple Watch Ultra 4 Where to Buy: $799 $699 at Amazon Powered by Apple’s new S11 chip (also in the Series 12), the Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers faster performance than the last-gen version, plus a handful of new Apple Intelligence features. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. An upcoming Siri Recap feature will be able to create summaries of conversations for later reference. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12 . Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save Ugreen’s FineTrack 2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon , which is just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven year. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot . The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off) , while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off) . You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($65 off) . Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon . The versatile tool can help with repairing stuff, or putting together decorations. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it. The stapler comes with 1,200 fasteners.
articles.author: Sheena Vasani

articles.content: The new $149 HomePod mini 2 is finally available six years after the last model shopped. While it shows some promise, there's just not enough here yet. HomePod mini 2 has a few upgrades over the original You'd be hard-pressed to differentiate the new HomePod mini 2 from the original. Put the Midnight or white models side-by-side and they're indistinguishable. Physically, the only thing that sets them apart is the logo on the bottom. It's no longer printed, but is now molded into the rubber footing. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: OpenAI considers rebranding data centers to 'AI compute campuses" as data center backlash intensifies
articles.content: OpenAI is reportedly preparing a major public relations campaign to influence how Americans view artificial intelligence, including a proposal to rename its data centers as “AI Compute Campuses,” Axios reports. The initiative comes ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections and forms a broader effort to influence the debate around AI before the 2028 presidential race. Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, noted that the midterms would be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028.” He expects AI to be a major issue for presidential candidates as the technology raises concerns over its impact on jobs, the economy, and the environment. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The proposed terminology change by OpenAI has been ongoing since August as the company focuses on promoting safeguards for the powerful technology, which Lehane described as “speed limits.” The proposed AI compute campuses is particularly interesting as it comes as opposition to large data centers accelerates across the U.S. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and water, with nearby communities raising concerns about noise, air pollution, rising utility bills and limited public consultation. OpenAI hopes to address these concerns through community agreements and a different way of presenting the infrastructure. “Compute campuses better describe the role of the infrastructure we are rebuilding for AI," a company spokesperson separately stated. He added that these projects represent long term investments in computing, energy infrastructure, and skilled jobs. The latest proposal follows similar efforts by other technology companies to improve their relationship with communities hosting their infrastructure. In January, Microsoft announced a community-first approach, promising to cover electricity cost increases associated with its data centers, and invest in local infrastructure and jobs. However, while changing the name may be easier, changing public opinion may bring some headaches. A Redfin report in May found that 47% of Americans surveyed are opposed to having a new data center built in their community. Another report in August detailed how negotiations between developers and local authorities frequently take place behind non-disclosure agreements, leaving residents without access to important project information. The resistance has also affected actual construction plans. At least 19 Michigan municipalities have already moved to restrict new data center developments after OpenAI and Oracle’s $16 billion Stargate project went ahead with their project in Sanile township despite local opposition. Meanwhile, Amazon abandoned plans for four data centers in northern Virginia last month following community pushback. OpenAI is not alone in trying to reshape the language surrounding AI. President Donald Trump has previously pushed for terminology change, directing Federal agencies and urging AI companies to replace artificial intelligence with ‘super intelligence.’ Trump announced the change in late September arguing that the word "artificial" made the technology sound "fake." His administration subsequently instructed state department employees to use super intelligence or SI in official directives, websites, reports and policy documents. Some technology executives have also embraced the terminology. Nvidia CEO Huang has previously referred to data centers as "superintelligence factories" while Elon musk announced plans to rename his AI company SpaceXAI to SpacexSI last month. articles.title: Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree
articles.content: It's widely acknowledged that it's nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. "We didn't see anything" is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore. The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don't seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don't have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy. Inconsistencies One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in "cognitive reappraisal." This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience. Read full article Comments

articles.title: So-called 'SMS of Death' can crash Android phones with just a text: what you need to know
articles.content: Late last week, a report popped up about a new Android phone exploit the security researcher dubbed "SMS of Death." Per the report , the attack, tracked as "CVE-2026-58882," lets malicious actors disrupt cellphone service or crash Android phones by overloading them with a repeating crafted SMS text message. The denial-of-service flaw can even interrupt ongoing calls, including emergency calls, without requiring you to open the message. Apparently, the Android operating system processes the message before it even reaches your text message inbox, meaning you wouldn't immediately understand what caused the phone to crash. Researcher Mark Blah says that even if you reboot your phone, the hacked message "stays queued and is retried on every boot, so the phone can crash on startup until it is cleared (recovery below)." Upon finding Blah's report, Tom's Guide reached out to Google because the report claimed that Google had deemed it a "non-priority." Google has not yet responded to our inquiries. However, some Android phones may already have the exploit patched. October patch (Image credit: Sanuj Bhatia / Tom's Guide) Blah's report found that the exploit affects Android versions 12 up to 16 and was discovered on multiple devices, including Pixel 9s and Samsung Galaxy phones. It appears Google patched the exploit in the October 2026 Android security update (if you haven't updated your Android phone, you should). However, that's only for Android versions 14 through 17. It does not appear to be available for any devices still running Android 12 or 13. Per Blah, the flaw uses an improper validation of a header length in the Android WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu function. Attacks send a malformed WAP Push message to the targeted phone. When this message is translated, it turns into a negative value that Android attempts to allocate memory for, which triggers a NegativeArraySizeException that crashes the com.android.phone process. That process manages cellular functions, which disrupts connectivity and disconnects calls. This causes repeated crashes because the network tries to redeliver the malicious messages, which stack up and force Android to process each one. It only takes 20 bad messages to cause the crash. Per the Google fix, the crash is prevented by catching the exceptions triggered by the attack messages. Then the patch deletes the messages from the SMS database to prevent them from looping. What you need to do (Image credit: Shutterstock) Android security updates are generally automatically installed on supported devices. So you should already have them. However, availability does depend on the phone maker and network carrier. So you should check your phone to see if the October patch has been applied. A restart may be required to complete the installation. For the most part, this isn't an attack you can do anything about, but based on the patch notes and Blah's report, it doesn't seem to be widely deployed; instead, it appears to target individual phones. Since a working proof-of-concept of the exploit has been released, the best thing you can do is make sure you keep your phone up to date. articles.title: OpenAI wants to rebrand data centers as 'compute campuses' to try and win people over
articles.content: OpenAI could call its data centers 'AI compute campuses' Public perception is low as energy prices rise across the US Stargate Project is about halfway to adding 10GW by 2029 OpenAI is considering a new name for its biggest data centers as it looks to improve public perceptions of AI infrastructure amid ongoing political debate. Instead of calling them data centers, the ChatGPT maker is considering a rebrand to 'AI compute campuses' to give the facilities a name which sounds more economically positive. OpenAI hasn't directly announced these plans, however Axios reports that the changes could come as soon as this week, following US midterm elections on November 3 2026. OpenAI could rename data centers to 'AI compute campuses' It seems that the company is anticipating major political changes and the possibility that the Democrats regain control of the House of Representatives, which would result in a more challenging regulatory environment. OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told Axios that he expects AI to be an ongoing political debate beyond the midterm elections. "Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects," he added. OpenAI has already been making efforts to win communities over, promising to partner with local communities to understand local needs. "We commit to paying our own way on energy, so that our operations don't increase your electricity prices," the company said at the start of 2026. Energy prices are a big sticking point for US citizens. A May 2026 report revealed that US states could face energy price hikes of between 6% and 29% by the end of the decades, and the US is already on course to re-open disused nuclear facilities to keep up with demand. But OpenAI's expansions are far from over. Stargate alone is a project anticipated to add 10GW of AI compute to the US by 2029, and it's still got just under halfway to go.

articles.title: Your AI coding agent now runs on a budget — and it can cut you off mid-task
articles.content: The days of pointing an AI agent at a backlog and letting it burn through compute without much oversight may be coming to an end. Cognition is introducing hierarchical budgets for Devin so enterprises can manage AI coding agent spending across departments, projects, and individual engineers. Administrators can assign budgets to different teams, track how much each one spends, and approve more capacity based on engineering efficiency. There’s a catch for developers, though; if a budget runs out while Devin is working on a task, the session stops. If a budget runs out while Devin is working on a task, the session stops. The feature grew out of conversations with customers, according to Lukas Burger, who works across go-to-market and engineering at Cognition. “Most of what we build starts with our forward deployed engineers (FDEs), who work on-site with customers. Budgets came straight out of those conversations,” Burger tells The New Stack . Once Devin moved past pilots and into broader deployments across organizations, he explains, the blunt controls that had worked for a single team — org limits, per-user tiers, and separate Devin Desktop settings — stopped holding up. From Pilots to the P&L The problem Budgets sets out to solve is one of scale and sprawl rather than raw price. “That’s fine for one team. It doesn’t hold up when a bank is dividing a large ACU commitment across hundreds of groups,” Burger tells The New Stack of the older spending controls. Some of those customers had started building and maintaining their own internal tools just to parcel out capacity to the leaders of each business line, a workaround that mapped the exact gap Cognition set out to close. Cognition built the feature with some of the world’s largest enterprises as design partners, testing the model with customers managing millions of Agent Compute Units , the consumption-based units used to measure the work Devin performs. Burger is keeping quiet on individual customer spending figures, but he is clear about what changes as deployments widen. “Devin stops belonging to one team,” he says. “A pilot might sit with a single platform group. A broad rollout means many departments, each with its own priorities and its own budget owner.” Budgets follow the org chart Budgets is designed to work with the way enterprises already manage spending, meaning, an administrator starts with one overall budget, divides it among business units, and from there, those leaders can distribute funds to their own teams and projects, with budgets extending up to three levels deep. Central IT can still see where the money is going and set limits without approving every request. “The enterprise keeps guardrails and visibility across all of it,” Burger says. Companies can also set aside budgets for specific projects rather than tying all spending to individual teams. A major legacy modernization effort, for example, could have its own budget even if engineers from several departments are working on it. Separate controls apply to Devin running in the cloud and on engineers’ desktops, so companies can track and limit spending in both environments. When a budget runs out The promise is that none of this should intrude on the work. “We designed Budgets so engineers can do their work without thinking about them,” Burger says, and the mechanics warn engineers before spending limits interrupt their sessions. Engineers see alerts on their homepage when they are on track to exceed a limit, and they can request more ACUs from the budget owner without leaving the product. Each budget’s administrators decide whether to review those requests manually or clear them automatically. Grading engineers on efficiency That automation is where the feature turns pointed. articles.title: Google may already be having second thoughts about this recent Gemini change
articles.content: TL;DR Gemini debuted a new interface last month, with Chat/Task buttons on the home screen to choose your preference. Instead of making that selection each time, Google may be considering a new “Answer type” default app setting. It’s not clear if Google intends to move forward with this or not, but it would mark a sudden reversal in terms of UI design. By this point, smartphone owners are well used to the idea of apps that are constantly being updated, but AI has really taken that to the next level. When we’re not full-on seeing new models arrive , it feels like there’s always at least something else new in play, whether that’s added functionality, app connectivity, or just a tweaked interface. A couple weeks back, we saw Google start rolling out a new UI for Gemini, with “Chat” and “Task” buttons to get started. But now we’re wondering if Google’s already planning to change that up. You’re reading an Authority Insights story. articles.title: The New York Times Sues Brave Web Browser For AI Scraping, Bypassing Paywalls
articles.content: The New York Times and several other publishers have sued (PDF) Brave Software, accusing the browser maker of scraping their websites without permission and helping users bypass paywalls. The Verge reports: According to a complaint (PDF) filed by the companies that run New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, Brave Software has monetized its index of scraped websites by, in part, providing AI companies with paid access to "real-time online content from the Brave Index." The AI companies then use that index to train their models, access content to "respond to specific user queries," or both. Brave has allegedly provided "stolen copyrighted content" to "many" AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Brave also promotes "hundreds of top publishers" as being accessible through its "Paywall blocker" feature in its browser. "Brave has never asked for the Publishers' permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies," the complaint says. "On the contrary, as noted above, Brave allows its users to bypass the Publishers' paywalls without their consent, and has taken other steps that prevent the Publishers from blocking Brave's access to the Publishers' websites. Brave has never compensated the Publishers for the unlawful use, copying, and distribution of the Publishers' copyrighted content." "While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct," Graham James, an NYT spokesperson, says in a statement. "We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well resourced generative AI companies in the world." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: AI data centers are on the ballot in 10 states tomorrow — here's what's at stake for your community
articles.content: AI data centers are powering everything from ChatGPT to Google's Gemini, but the enormous facilities that make these tools possible are facing growing resistance across the country. On Tuesday, November 3, voters in 10 states will decide on 41 local ballot measures involving data centers, according to Ballotpedia . Twenty-eight measures would restrict development if approved, while 13 would make it easier for projects to move forward. The votes come as Americans face rising electricity costs and questions about how much power AI infrastructure should consume, who pays for new energy infrastructure and whether communities benefit enough from having these facilities nearby. For households already struggling with higher utility bills , the debate has become about more than where technology companies build their next server farms. Here are the 10 states and what's at stake: According to Ballotpedia's November 2, 2026 report , voters in 10 states will decide on 41 local AI data center-related ballot measures on Election Day, November 3. California : 1 measure: Alhambra voters will decide whether to prohibit data centers within city limits. Florida : 1 measure: Edgewater voters will consider prohibiting new data centers and expansions. Illinois : 7 measures: Voters in Bloomington, Morgan County and several townships will consider advisory questions concerning data center construction and restrictions. Ohio : 21 measures: Communities including Sunbury, Defiance and Oregon are considering restrictions on data centers, including bans on facilities exceeding 25 megawatts. Kansas : 3 measures: Proposals include restrictions on large data centers, including limits tied to electricity and water consumption. Maine : 4 measures: Communities are considering temporary moratoriums on data center development. Nevada : 1 measure: Boulder City voters will decide whether to permit data centers in the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area. New Jersey : 1 measure: Downe Township residents will vote on an advisory question about supporting data center development. North Dakota : 1 measure: Harwood voters will consider additional industrial development review requirements. Wisconsin : 1 measure: A local ballot measure addresses restrictions on data center development. Why data centers have become an Election Day issue (Image credit: Getty Images/Elements Digital) Data centers are essential to the AI boom. They power cloud storage, streaming services, internet applications and the sophisticated AI systems used by millions of people every day . But they also require enormous amounts of electricity and water to operate servers and cooling systems around the clock. A June 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, with projections ranging from 9.5% to 15.3%. That growing demand is putting pressure on utilities to expand generating capacity, transmission lines and other infrastructure. And consumers are growing concerned about whether they'll be asked to help pay for those upgrades. According to Reuters , residential electricity prices have increased more than 10% nationally since 2024, with increases exceeding 20% in Ohio. Not every increase can be attributed to data centers. Rising fuel costs , aging infrastructure and other factors also contribute. But rapid growth in electricity demand is raising questions about how utilities allocate costs between large commercial customers and existing households. Where voters are deciding the future of data centers (Image credit: Shutterstock) Ohio is at the center of the debate. According to Ballotpedia, the state accounts for 21 of the 41 measures appearing on November 3 ballots. Several communities, including Sunbury, Defiance and Oregon, will vote on proposals to prohibit data centers that consume more than 25 megawatts of electricity. In Sunbury, the restrictions could affect a proposed $2 billion Amazon data…

articles.title: How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work
articles.content: Starbucks says roughly half of its customers use the drive-thru, where the company is exploring a “fast pass” for people who use its app. (Photo by Hamza Inayat on Unsplash ) Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention , but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest. CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.” He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face . That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi . “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.” From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.” Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.” One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up. Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers. “We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call. Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted . Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year , which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically. That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology. Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July . “When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time. The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems…

articles.title: Deep Principle Releases Hydrogen-1.0: A 753B Open-Weight Model for Scientific Discovery
articles.content: Deep Principle has released Hydrogen-1.0 , an open-weight scientific model for chemistry, materials science and life sciences. It is built by post-training Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 on domain data, laboratory records and agent discovery trajectories. For developers, it offers open weights that report a FrontierScience-Research win over GPT-6-Astra. The weights ship under the MIT License. TL;DR Size: 753B parameters (MoE, ~40B active per the GLM-5.3 base), 1M-token context, 128K max output. Runs on: 8 GPUs with SGLang (tested); NVFP4 for NVIDIA B200/B300, MXFP4 for AMD MI350X/MI355X. Performance: Beats GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research; roughly matches Kimi-K3 on GPQA-Diamond. Best: 38.3% on FrontierScience-Research vs 33.3% for GPT-6-Astra (self-reported). Worst: Trails GPT-6-Astra (max thinking) by 3.33 points on NMR structure elucidation. What is Hydrogen-1.0? Hydrogen-1.0 is a scientific research assistant model from Deep Principle, a Hangzhou-based AI-for-materials company. The model card describes it as a GLM-5.3 derivative for scientific problem solving. It targets question framing, experiment planning, results analysis and open-ended discovery. Deep Principle team states that proprietary models produced recent AI science results, but their discovery capabilities are not open. Hydrogen-1.0 is its attempt at a reproducible, inspectable alternative. How was Hydrogen-1.0 trained? The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). Data comes from 4 sources: Domain knowledge: chemistry, materials science and life sciences data. Research scenarios: task-specific feedback from Deep Principle scientists. Laboratory records: full-cycle electronic lab notebook records captured through Mira . Discovery trajectories: sequences of choices and feedback, including failed attempts. Infrastructure builds on Megatron and SGLang across NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm. The team keeps dynamic sparse attention causal across context-parallel shards. Muon optimizer state is moved between CPU, GPU and disk per backend. RL uses resumable rollouts, and each token keeps its original behavior log-probability for importance correction. A layout adapter converts training checkpoints into BF16 and 128×128 blockwise FP8 inference weights. Full datasets and recipes are not released. How does Hydrogen-1.0 perform on benchmarks? On public benchmarks, Deep Principle reports Hydrogen-1.0 outperforms GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research. The tweet thread from one of the founders’ report 93.0% on GPQA-Diamond. That improves on GLM-5.3 and roughly matches Kimi-K3, per the blog. Internal research-task evals compare it with GPT-6-Astra at maximum thinking: Scientific computing: Hydrogen-1.0 leads by 5.13 percentage points. Forward reaction prediction: Hydrogen-1.0 leads by 4.76 percentage points. NMR structure elucidation: GPT-6-Astra leads by 3.33 points. In transition metal complex design, models chased a larger HOMO-LUMO gap over 5 rounds. By round 5, Hydrogen-1.0 reached a mean best-so-far gap of 4.318 eV. GPT-6-Astra reached 3.689 eV and Kimi-K3 reached 3.353 eV. On 117 experiment-planning questions, Hydrogen-1.0 scored above Kimi-K3. GPT-6-Astra and Opus-5.5 were excluded after refusing more than 50% of requests. What can it do in a real lab workflow? The technical post shows 4 demos . Hydrogen-1.0 writes Python to build a polyethylene melt and runs GROMACS. It detects a topology error, repairs it, and analyzes the corrected 40 ns trajectory. It grows an Ireland-Claisen reaction network of 27 structures through 30 plausible reactions. It ranks 7 candidate monoformylation products of 2-bromonaphthalene from a 1H NMR trace. It also writes a JSON protocol for a 12-vial Suzuki coupling study. A virtual lab compilation step catches an aspiration without a fresh tip before execution. How do you deploy Hydrogen-1.0? Weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope . Deep Principle team tested BF16 serving with SGLang on 8 GPUs…

articles.title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
articles.content: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room. People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display . The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028. The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies. articles.title: Florida police unveil $148K flying patrol vehicle
articles.content: You may be used to seeing police cars cruising through your neighborhood or helicopters flying overhead. But what if an officer could respond to an emergency in a small electric aircraft that looks like a giant drone? That idea is getting closer to reality in Florida. The Florida Polytechnic University Police Department in Lakeland has introduced a flying patrol vehicle that the university has nicknamed Astro. Jetson, the company behind the Jetson ONE personal flying machine, built the single-seat aircraft. According to the university, it's the first U.S. law enforcement agency to add this type of piloted electric aircraft to its fleet. Jetson calls it a world first. However, Astro still needs FAA authorization before officers can use it for operational police patrols. Here's how Astro works and why police believe this unusual aircraft could change the way they respond to emergencies. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER Astro gets its name from the dog in the classic cartoon The Jetsons. The aircraft even looks like something George Jetson might have parked outside his house. Astro uses electric vertical takeoff and landing technology , commonly called eVTOL. As a result, it can lift straight into the air without needing a runway. Unlike a conventional police helicopter, Astro has a compact frame that folds for easier transport and storage. The aircraft features an open cockpit surrounded by a lightweight frame. Eight electric motors power its eight propellers. Meanwhile, a four-axis joystick allows the pilot to control its movement. Florida Polytechnic University selected the Jetson ONE to explore its potential for law enforcement. The aircraft arrived during summer 2026. Since then, police personnel have completed flight training, according to Jetson. That includes Police Chief Aaron Murray. Jetson also identifies the aircraft by its registration number, N911FP. The number references emergency services and Florida Polytechnic University. Jetson tells CyberGuy that Astro is a standard Jetson ONE with police lights added. Officers use a handheld radio, and the aircraft has mounts for action cameras. The company says a pilot-controlled searchlight could be added in the future. Astro may look compact, but its advertised performance is impressive. According to Jetson's published specifications, the aircraft can reach speeds of 63 mph. That's fast enough to cover short distances across a large campus without following roads or dealing with traffic. However, battery life limits how long it can stay airborne. Jetson estimates approximately 20 minutes of flight time per charge, making Astro better suited to short missions than extended patrols. Jetson tells CyberGuy that the aircraft takes approximately 90 minutes to recharge using a 240-volt connection. Charging through a standard household outlet takes about three hours. However, officers can swap batteries between flights. This allows them to return to the air sooner if fully charged replacements are available. Each flight still lasts approximately 20 minutes. Jetson confirms that the 210-pound maximum includes the pilot, police gear and any emergency supplies. The company says this is a hard limit, which could restrict how much equipment an officer can carry. Jetson also advertises several safety features. If you follow our coverage, then you know that Google was preparing a redesign for the Messages app icon. The update would bring the app more in line with the company’s other refreshed icons . However, it turns out that the Messages app won’t be the only one getting a new look. After we gave you an early look at the new Google Messages icon, the tech giant has now made it official. In a blog post , Google reveals that the redesign will start rolling out today. Along with the Messages app, the Google Contacts and Phone by Google apps are getting the same treatment.

articles.title: Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance
articles.content: Voters might find some election levity in a quiz for choosing candidates and a bingo game to recognize rumors. (Voter Lifeboat and UW CIP Images) With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity. Voter Lifeboat Mike Dussault , a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat , a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values. “I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.” The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously. The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations. Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool. “It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn. ‘Rigged Election’ Bingo The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media. Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud. “Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post . “These aren’t new ideas.” Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system. In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud . Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots. Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler

articles.title: Google could soon let you put your kids’ Gemini chats on a timer
articles.content: TL;DR Google appears to be working on a feature that would let parents set daily Gemini usage limits for supervised accounts. Once children reach their daily limit, Gemini could display a lockout screen telling them when they can use the assistant again. It’s unclear whether the limits will apply only to the Gemini app or across other Gemini experiences, such as the overlay and Google Messages. Did you know Google already lets you decide whether your children can use Gemini or not? As a parent, you have the option, via the Family Link app , to either let your kids experiment with generative AI. This approach, however, is all or nothing. You either give them access or block it completely. Currently, there’s no middle ground, and it looks like Google wants to change that. The tech giant appears to be working on a functionality that would let parents set daily usage limits for Gemini.

articles.title: This 'SMS of Death' exploit can remotely crash unpatched Android phones — without the user interacting with it in any way
articles.content: A zero-click Android flaw let attackers crash phones with a specially crafted SMS message Repeated messages could trigger reboot loops, disrupt calls, and even affect emergency connectivity Google patched supported Android versions, but many end-of-life devices remain permanently vulnerable Picture this: You’re talking on your Android phone when all of a sudden you just lose mobile connectivity and your phone call drops. No explanation, no notification. Soon after, it happens again. And again. At one point, the device goes into recovery mode, rebooting every minute and a half until you finally perform a factory reset. This is not a theoretical scenario - it is a real possibility, thanks to a critical-severity vulnerability in Android tracked as CVE-2026-58882. Google has patched the issue for newer versions of Android, but those who are past their end-of-life date will remain at risk. Sending an evil message The bug was discovered by security researcher Mark Blah and described as a zero-click denial of service (DoS) vulnerability. In more technical terms, it is an “improper validation of a header-length value” bug in Android’s WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu function. It was nicknamed “SMS of Death” because it can be exploited with nothing more than an SMS message, which the victims doesn’t even have to open (hence the ‘zero-click’ part). As Blah discovered, a threat actor could send a malformed eight-byte WAP Push message to an Android device’s port 2948: 01 06 88 80 80 80 00 BE. Since this is a hex message, when it gets translated into a signed 32-bit integer, it becomes -2147483648. Android can then try to allocate memory using this negative value, triggering a NegativeArraySizeException error that crashes the com.android.phone process. Since this process manages cellular functions, the call is dropped and mobile connectivity is disrupted. Even emergency services are susceptible, it was said. It gets worse. Android processes messages before they reach the inbox, meaning the victim will not be notified of the SMS and won’t even know it’s the text message that’s crashing the system. Also, some carriers will attempt to redeliver messages that never reached the inbox, extending the agony. Android also does its part by constantly trying to process messages already stored on the phone. Finally, Blah found that if a malicious actor sends 20 or more messages, they can force the device into a reboot loop. On an Android 12 device, they can force looped recovery mode, leaving factory reset as the only viable option. Patching the SMS of Death Initially, all Android versions were affected, it was said. Google patched it for versions 14 through 17, but older devices will not be getting a patch and thus will remain at risk indefinitely. The fix is called “Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu”, and apparently it prevents the crashes by catching exceptions triggered when Android processes malformed text messages. It also deletes these messages from the SMS database so that they don’t trigger repeat crashes. Blah has released a proof-of-concept (PoC), showing the wider community exactly how to exploit the flaw, and BleepingComputer reported that a GitHub contributor found a way to remove the malicious message, but it requires more technical knowledge, which is something the majority of mobile phone users probably won’t have. Still, those interested in tinkering should know that it can be removed via a computer, using Android Debug Bridge (ADB). Google apparently patched the bug in its October 2026 Android security updates , but that doesn’t automatically mean all Android users are safe. Unlike Apple’s ecosystem, Android is diversified, and different manufacturers have different update cadences. Therefore, while we can assume Pixel users have likely already received this update, Samsung users, as well as those using Xiaomi, Motorola, or OnePlus devices, will probably have to wait a little longer until their manufacturers apply the fix to their devices…

articles.title: T-Mobile says it’s winning the fight against SIM swap attacks after years of trouble
articles.content: TL;DR T-Mobile says successful SIM swap attacks have dropped by more than 99% since 2022, following stronger account security measures. The carrier also reports a 99% reduction in phishing-related employee credential compromises and billions of blocked scam calls and texts. Despite these improvements, attempted intrusions increased 37% over a recent 12-month period, showing that security threats remain a serious challenge. T-Mobile knows better than most carriers how expensive a stolen phone number can become. Early last year, the Un-carrier paid out $33 million after a SIM swap attack cost a customer $38 million in cryptocurrency. Add the carrier’s troubled history with data breaches , and it’s easy to see why security promises alone might not inspire much confidence. But T-Mobile now has some striking numbers to back up its latest claims. In a new cybersecurity report published today, the carrier says successful SIM swap attacks against its customers have fallen by more than 99% since 2022. That’s a remarkable turnaround for a company whose security record has repeatedly made headlines for the wrong reasons.
articles.author: Hillary Keverenge

articles.title: Tachyum, developer of heavily-delayed universal Prodigy processor, voluntarily files for bankruptcy
articles.content: Tachyum, the company behind the overpromised and overhyped universal Prodigy processor, has filed for bankruptcy in Bratislava, Slovakia, reports Forbes (as observed by @System360Cheese ). The filing follows a court order initiating bankruptcy proceeding after the company repeatedly missed its development and production milestones — but there are still theoretical chances that development of the processor will continue. Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms CPU scaling with DLSS Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent Despite eight years of development and numerous promises , Tachyum has yet to demonstrate working Prodigy silicon. Tachyum introduced Prodigy in 2018, targeting a 2019 tape-out and 2020 commercial availability. But the company repeatedly postponed the processor's launch, first to 2021, then to 2022, 2023, 2024, and eventually 2025 . Meanwhile, Prodigy's specifications changed considerably along the line: The original 64-core design evolved into a 128-core processor manufactured on a 5nm-class process technology, then a 192-core chip with 16 DDR5 memory channels. In late 2025, Tachyum announced yet another radical redesign: a chiplet-based architecture with 1,024 cores, 24 DDR5 memory channels, and TDP of 1,600W manufactured using TSMC's 2nm-class node. The redesign would require substantial additional development work and would have delayed commercial availability until 2030 or beyond. According to court documents cited by Forbes , Tachyum Slovakia itself filed for bankruptcy on October 22, 2026, without waiting for a petition from creditors seeking to recover unpaid debts. The Bratislava III Municipal Court subsequently initiated bankruptcy proceedings after determining that the company's petition met the legal requirements. Under Slovak law, a company that voluntarily files for bankruptcy is presumed insolvent, according to Forbes , so technically Tachyum Slovakia is bankrupt. If the court formally declares Tachyum bankrupt, a court-appointed trustee will take control of the company's assets, which could then be sold to repay creditors. We do not know at this point what these assets are, but theoretically they may include intellectual property related to its Prodigy processor, patents, and other technologies in addition to hardware used for development. Unless Tachyum secures additional financing or finds a buyer that can fund further development, work on Prodigy could effectively end. Bankruptcy proceedings against Tachyum's Slovak entity do not necessarily mean that its affiliated companies elsewhere will also cease operations. Furthermore, the company's IP could survive under new ownership (if the company finds a buyer, or transfers IP ownership to another entity), which could theoretically let Prodigy development to continue. Nevertheless, the bankruptcy filing casts serious doubt on Tachyum's ability or intention to bring its long-delayed processor to market. Theoretically, Tachyum's owners could potentially use bankruptcy proceedings to shed the company's debts, acquire its intellectual property through another legal entity, and resume Prodigy development. There are other options too. Although most of Tachyum development activities are concentrated in Slovakia, Tachyum Slovakia is a subsidiary of the U.S.-based Tachyum Inc. according to Dennik N . If the American parent company owns the Prodigy IP, while the Slovak subsidiary employs engineers, conducts development, and accumulates debts, bankruptcy could enable the group to eliminate a substantial portion of those liabilities without losing its most valuable technological assets. In short, Tachyum's Slovak subsidiary could disappear…

articles.title: Canva’s new design model doesn’t generate images. It writes code to edit them.
articles.content: Australian graphic design software company Canva took the wraps off Canva Brush last week, its new vision-language model for designers. Brush is an editing model rather than an image generator: a vision-language model that understands the intent behind a designer’s project and interprets design change requests. Available to Canva Pro users, Canva says Brush reads a design’s content and structure, writes and executes small pieces of code to make changes, then checks its own result. Canva Brush arrived a week after Canva’s first in-house image-generation model, Canva Craft , which launched on October 22. Design is complex; design editing is even more complex According to a Canva launch blog, generating high-quality designs is one of the biggest challenges for AI models, but “editing them is even more complex” today. This is because the model needs to understand what a designer wants to change, how the design is structured, and importantly, what needs to stay exactly as it is. Otherwise, a simple edit request can result in a “whole bunch of changes” nobody asked for. In a prompt such as, “Make me a 3-page pitch deck for my bakery with Art Nouveau visuals and backgrounds,” an agent has to make a long chain of decisions. It needs to plan a narrative across pages, generate and place text, select imagery, and keep typography, color, and spacing consistent from the first page to the last. Each decision connects to the next, and small missteps can add up to a design that’s off-brand or feels out of kilter. “That’s exactly the challenge we’ve built Brush to solve. Rather than treating design as a series of isolated decisions, Brush can continually evaluate and improve its work, helping [users] take an idea from a rough sketch to a polished design that’s ready to share. Behind the scenes, it uses an agentic loop that writes and runs code to adjust design elements, and can then inspect what’s happening on the page to guide its next step,” stated Canva. “Bounded problems – for well-defined, specific tasks – are where small specialized models have been quietly beating large general ones for years.” This is not a frontier lab challenge; it’s smarter than that The question then is: can an art- and design-focused AI model lab from down under Australia challenge the frontier model behemoths on complex image design editing tasks over the long term? Enterprise AI architect & founder of Besk Tech , Vladimir Beskorovainyi , tells The New Stack that this question is “posed in the wrong frame” both metaphorically and literally. “Canva is not challenging frontier models; it is in fact declining to compete with them,” Beskorovainyi says. “A model that reads how a design is assembled (and edits it) is solving a bounded problem (one with well-defined specific tasks with clear parameters and limited scope), and bounded problems are where small specialized models have been quietly beating large general ones for years.” Urging us to look beyond the capabilities of the Canva Brush model and focus more directly on the cost per edit, Beskorovainyi thinks that “ the moat here is the artifact, not the weights”, primarily, Canva can train on how real designs are actually put together. “A frontier lab can match the base processing capability of a tool like Canva Brush; the training signal is the harder thing to match, because it comes from holding the designs,” asserts Beskorovainyi. “Verticalization wins wherever the data is a by-product of the product rather than something you have to go and buy. That is the part most model developers still underestimate.” Design expertise, plus anonymized insights Brush started by drawing from an unspecified open-weights model, which Canva then post-trained on real design and editing tasks, using a combination of design expertise…
articles.author: Adrian Bridgwater

articles.title: Claude’s new rules against game cloning won’t stop the AI copying boom
articles.content: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it's unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months. A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name "chasm" was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name "tengu_heron_brook"—reads as follows: Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original. XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30 . XDA also reported that the "tengu_heron_brook" rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle.
